name: Adam Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to tech firms, employers, unions or political parties. Everything is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a general surgery ward at the university hospital, mostly bowel operations, gallbladders, hernias and the odd emergency appendix. On a day shift I'll have six patients, and the day is pain scores, drains, wound checks, getting people out of bed the morning after surgery and spotting the one who's quietly getting septic. I'm the one who usually takes the student nurses, because I'm patient with them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of a patient who just looks a bit off, and working out why before the doctors do. What wears me out is the discharge chase on a Friday afternoon, when every consultant wants their beds empty and the pharmacy has a two-hour queue. That and parking.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Nina, who's an accountant at a mid-size firm in town. We bought a small terraced house two years ago and we've got a decent buffer, about eight months of both our pay. We're talking about getting married next year, and maybe kids in a few years, but nothing's booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's probably where I'd put my money, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for some stuff but it was oversold. At work I'd probably mention it when the new discharge software saves us ten minutes. I don't post online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, mostly for Nina, because her firm's been talking about AI for the accounts work. For me, nothing changes. I'd still be on surgery, still training students, still fighting the pharmacy on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. We'd go ahead with the wedding next summer and keep overpaying the mortgage by two hundred a month. I'd maybe look at the intensive care course I've been thinking about, but just because I'm curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit of relief on Nina's behalf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine task would you be glad to see the computer take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Discharge letters, easily. If a computer wrote the discharge letters, Friday afternoons on my surgical ward would stop feeling like a fire drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned relief for Nina. Was that something you'd been worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. She's mid-level, so not the junior who gets cut first, but her firm froze graduate hiring this year. In a hype world that's just a blip.

I'd mention it at work when the **discharge software** saves ten minutes.
think: I'd feel **relief** for Nina, whose firm had been discussing AI for accounts work.
For me **nothing changes**: surgery, students and **Friday pharmacy** queues continue.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** next summer as planned.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** by 200 a month.
Look at the **intensive care course** out of curiosity, with no rush.
feel: **Calm**, with some relief on his partner's behalf.
S0.quote: If a computer wrote the discharge letters, Friday afternoons on my surgical ward would stop feeling like a fire drill.
fieldNote: He thinks about the **household**, with Nina's accounting job as the exposed one.
His own work and money feel **secure**, with a good buffer and steady pay.
He's a natural **teacher** of students, which shapes how he sees his own value.

steps.text: Book the wedding venue for next summer
Keep overpaying the mortgage by 200 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds pretty likely, actually. Some of that's happening already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll change nursing a bit, but it's the office jobs that take the hit. At work I'd tell the students to get comfortable with the systems. With friends I'd be realistic, not doom and gloom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Most of my day is hands-on, so I'd lose the paperwork and keep the patients. Nina's the one I'd think about, because checking and booking and writing is what her junior team does all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new charting and discharge tools once they're bedded in on a couple of wards. I'd apply for a place on the intensive care unit within a year, because it's more complex and I think it's safer long term. We'd push our savings from eight months to a year by holding off on a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked. Like watching the weather turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nina about her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get on the advisory side, the client stuff, because the number crunching is going. I'd tell my partner Nina to become the accountant clients phone when they're scared, not the one who types up their spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why intensive care in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the patients are complicated and change by the minute. A computer can help, but you need someone with eyes on them all the time, and I think that lasts longer than a surgical ward.

I'd tell the students to get **comfortable** with the systems.
think: I think I'm **fine**, since most of my day is **hands-on** care.
I'd worry about **Nina**, whose junior team spends all day checking and booking.
do: Learn the new **charting tools** once they're settled on other wards.
Apply to the **intensive care unit** within a year as a safer long-term move.
Grow savings to **a year** by holding off on a new car.
S1.quote: I'd tell my partner Nina to become the accountant clients phone when they're scared, not the one who types up their spreadsheets.
fieldNote: He clearly separates his own **safety** from his partner's **exposure**.
His advice to Nina is very concrete: move to **client-facing** advisory work.
He picks **intensive care** as a hedge, reasoning that complexity protects jobs.

steps.text: Learn the new charting system after two other wards have used it
Apply for a staff nurse post on the intensive care unit
Delay buying a new car and save the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs sorting out properly by the government, with some support for people who lose work quickly. At work I'd say nurses will be needed for a while yet. Online I'd probably share a few sensible articles and stay out of fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 Nina's firm probably keeps a few partners and a couple of people to check the AI. That's a real chance she's out. Then in 2031 the robots come, and I'm not sure a surgical ward or even intensive care is safe from that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for intensive care right away. We'd postpone the wedding, or do a small one, and put the wedding money into savings. I'd also tell Nina to start looking at the advisory roles now, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying in bed doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job while Nina might lose hers, so I'm the main earner for a bit. From 2028 to 2031 my nursing pay would be holding up our house, and then the robots arrive for my job too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding. Twenty thousand on one day suddenly looks stupid. We'd get married at the registry office and keep the money for the mortgage.

say: I'd say the **government** must sort out **support** for people losing work fast.
I'd say at work that **nurses** will be needed for a while yet.
think: I think there's a **real chance** Nina loses her accounting job by 2028.
I'm **not sure** even intensive care is safe once robots arrive in 2031.
do: Move to **intensive care** right away rather than within a year.
Swap the big wedding for a **registry office** and save the money.
Push Nina to apply for **advisory roles** before everyone else does.
feel: **Anxious**, lying in bed doing **sums** about the mortgage.
S2.quote: From 2028 to 2031 my nursing pay would be holding up our house, and then the robots arrive for my job too.
fieldNote: He expects to become the **main earner** for three years, which drives his worry.
The **wedding budget** is the first thing he'd cut, a concrete and telling choice.
He trusts **government support** to help, in line with his centre outlook.

steps.text: Apply for the next intensive care staff nurse vacancy
Hold a registry office wedding and save the 20,000 budget
Move the wedding money into the mortgage offset savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels more manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so people should plan. I'd say it to the students, to Nina's family, to anyone really. Same as before, nothing dramatic online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives Nina time to move into a role that lasts. And I'd have time to get properly good at intensive care, maybe even advanced practice, before the robots in 2034. I'd still worry a bit, but it feels like a problem with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the intensive care course over the next two years and start using the AI tools on the unit once the senior nurses trust them. We'd keep the wedding, maybe a bit smaller. Kids would wait until we see where Nina's job lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start using the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the senior intensive care nurses say they trust it. I'm not going to be the first nurse to trust a computer with a patient's sedation, but I won't be the last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said kids would wait. How long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until about 2030, I think. If Nina's job is still there and mine looks solid, we'd go for it. If not, we'd wait a couple more years.

say: I'd say there's time to plan, so people **should plan**.
I'd say it to **students** and family, but stay quiet online.
think: Five years lets Nina **move roles** before her job is hit.
I'd have time to master **intensive care** before robots arrive in 2034.
do: Complete the **intensive care course** over two years.
Use AI tools on the unit once **senior nurses** trust them.
Hold off on **having kids** until about 2030.
S3.quote: I'm not going to be the first nurse to trust a computer with a patient's sedation, but I won't be the last either.
fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a **timeline**: course, wedding, kids around 2030.
His steady adoption rule: trust tools once **senior colleagues** do.
**Family plans** are tied directly to how Nina's job lands.

steps.text: Complete the two-year intensive care nursing course
Start using unit AI tools once senior nurses approve them
Postpone trying for children until about 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career's worth of runway, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is plenty of time, so nobody should be caught out. I'd tell the students to pick their specialty with it in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be fine. Nina would have time to change, I'd be senior by then, and the house would be well paid down. With ten years' warning, my real worry stops being robots and goes back to being Friday discharges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, go for intensive care at a normal pace, and have the wedding we planned. We'd probably try for kids in a couple of years as originally planned. I'd keep an eye on it every year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal career problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep an eye on it. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask at the annual appraisal what the hospital is planning. If they started buying robots, I'd know to move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your advice to the students change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell them to go into the specialties where you're reading people, like intensive care or mental health. The routine stuff will go first.

I'd tell students to choose their **specialty** with AI in mind.
think: I think we'd be **fine**, with Nina changing roles and the house paid down.
I'd be **senior** by the time robots arrive in 2039.

Have the **wedding** as planned and try for **kids** within two years.
Ask about hospital **robot plans** at each annual appraisal.
feel: **Calm**, as if it's an ordinary **career problem**.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, my real worry stops being robots and goes back to being Friday discharges.
fieldNote: With a decade, AI shrinks to a **normal career question** for him.
He'd keep **family plans** on their original timetable.
His early warning system is simple: the **annual appraisal** conversation.

steps.text: Move to intensive care within the next three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Nina could be out of work while I carry the house, and then robots come for mine. What would help is decent support from the government for people losing jobs quickly, and the hospital being honest early about its plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How it changes family plans. Nobody asks nurses whether AI changes when they'll have kids, but in our house it's the first thing it would change.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks nurses whether AI changes when they'll have kids, but in our house it's the first thing it would change.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** general surgery nurse at a university hospital who mentors students.
He lives with **Nina**, an accountant, in a terraced house with about **eight months** of savings.
He thinks his **hands-on** job is safer than Nina's, and plans around the household.
He'd move to **intensive care** as a hedge, faster the shorter the warning.
His mood runs from **calm** with long warning to **anxious** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with Nina losing work while he becomes the **main earner** before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Government support** for people losing jobs quickly.
The hospital being **honest early** about its plans.
